nodes.title: Nested and Separate Loops
nodes.question: Look at the code below. What is the overall time complexity?
nodes.explanation: Step 1: Identify each loop separately. The first loop iterates through all n elements once, so it is O(n). Step 2: The second set of loops is nested — the outer loop runs n times and for each iteration the inner loop also runs n times, giving O(n × n) = O(n²). Step 3: When combining complexities, we take the dominant term. O(n) + O(n²) = O(n²) because n² grows much faster than n for large inputs.

options.text: O(n)
O(n log n)
O(n²)

nodes.title: Match Code Blocks to Big O
nodes.question: Match each code block with its correct time complexity.
nodes.explanation: Step 1: print(numbers[0]) accesses a single element at a fixed index — no loop, no scaling — so it is O(1) constant time. Step 2: 'for num in numbers: print(num)' iterates through every element exactly once, so it is O(n) linear time. Step 3: Nested loops (for i ... for j ...) iterate n × n times total, so it is O(n²) quadratic time. Step 4: 'while n > 1: n = n // 2' halves the input each iteration. The number of halvings needed to reach 1 is log₂(n), so it is O(log n) logarithmic time.

nodes.title: Stack vs Queue Operations
nodes.question: Consider the operations: Add A, Add B, Add C, Remove, Add D. Fill the blanks for both stack and queue behavior.
nodes.explanation: Step 1: Start with an empty structure. Add A, Add B, Add C in order. Step 2: For a Stack (LIFO — Last In, First Out), Remove takes the most recently added item, which is C. The stack now contains [A, B]. Add D, giving [A, B, D]. Step 3: For a Queue (FIFO — First In, First Out), Remove takes the oldest item, which is A. The queue now contains [B, C]. Add D, giving [B, C, D]. Key insight: Stack uses Pop (removes from top), Queue uses Dequeue (removes from front).

nodes.title: Find the Bug: Remove Nth Node From End
nodes.question: The code works for many cases, but it has a hidden bug. Which test case exposes the bug?

codeSnippet.code:
def remove_nth_from_end(head, n):
    fast = head
    slow = head
    prev = None

    for _ in range(n):
        fast = fast.next

    while fast:
        fast = fast.next
        prev = slow
        slow = slow.next

    prev.next = slow.next

    return head

nodes.explanation: When n equals the length of the list, the node to remove is the head. After moving fast n steps, fast is None, so the while loop does not run and prev stays None. Then prev.next causes an error. A complete solution should handle head removal, often with a dummy node.

nodes.title: BFS Visit Order
nodes.question: You are doing BFS on this tree. BFS visits nodes level by level. What is the correct BFS order?
nodes.explanation: Step 1: BFS (Breadth-First Search) uses a queue and visits all nodes at the current depth before moving to the next level. Step 2: Start at root A (level 0). Enqueue A's children: B and C (level 1). Step 3: Visit B, enqueue B's child D. Visit C, enqueue C's children E and F. Level 2 nodes are: D, E, F. Step 4: Visit D, E, F in order. All have no children, so the traversal ends. Final BFS order: A → B → C → D → E → F. Key insight: BFS always completes one level entirely before visiting the next.
